## Proof

Let the four disks be dropped independently with centers $X_1, X_2, X_3, X_4$ distributed i.i.d. according to a continuous distribution on a finite area $A \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ (uniform, or more generally any distribution absolutely continuous with respect to 2-dimensional Lebesgue measure). "The disks are collinear" means their four centers lie on a single straight line.

**Key observation.** If four points are collinear, then in particular any three of them are collinear. Hence

$$\Pr(\text{four collinear}) \;\le\; \Pr(X_1, X_2, X_3 \text{ collinear}).$$

It therefore suffices to show that three i.i.d. continuously-distributed points in the plane are collinear with probability $0$.

**Three points are collinear with probability 0.** Condition on $X_1$ and $X_2$. With probability $1$, $X_1 \neq X_2$, so they determine a unique line $\ell = \overleftrightarrow{X_1 X_2}$. The third point $X_3$ is independent of $(X_1, X_2)$ and has a distribution absolutely continuous w.r.t. Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^2$. A line $\ell$ is a 1-dimensional affine subspace, hence has 2-dimensional Lebesgue measure $0$. Therefore

$$\Pr(X_3 \in \ell \mid X_1, X_2) = 0 \quad \text{a.s.}$$

Integrating over $(X_1, X_2)$,

$$\Pr(X_1, X_2, X_3 \text{ collinear}) = 0.$$

**Conclusion.** Since collinearity of all four centers implies collinearity of the first three,

$$0 \;\le\; \Pr(\text{four disks collinear}) \;\le\; \Pr(X_1, X_2, X_3 \text{ collinear}) = 0.$$

Hence

$$\boxed{\Pr(\text{four randomly dropped disks are collinear}) = 0.}$$

The physical interpretation is that the centers are drawn from a continuous (non-atomic) distribution over a 2-dimensional region; requiring them to lie on a 1-dimensional subset (a line) imposes a measure-zero constraint. The "no overlap" condition only restricts the support of the joint distribution but does not introduce atoms, so the same measure-zero argument applies.
